value.kid_phrase: being brave even when you feel scared

story_world: Shushan (Susa), capital of the ancient Achaemenid Persian Empire. The king's palace: tall slender fluted stone columns topped with twin-bull capitals, wide flat-roofed halls and porches, cedar-beam ceilings, wide stone staircases, walls of glazed brick in turquoise, gold and cream with rows of rosettes and friendly striding lions, stepped crenellated parapets, rich purple and blue hangings, gold cups and low couches. Doorways are tall and rectangular with flat lintels. Gardens with date palms, pomegranate trees and straight water channels; warm sandstone and cream plaster under a deep blue sky. Royal robes with wide sleeves and sashes; crenellated golden crowns; cloth head wraps. No pointed or horseshoe arches, no domes, no mosaic tilework, no Star of David.

cards.image_prompt:
A magnificent golden Persian crown with a stepped, crenellated rim rests on a plush royal-purple velvet
cushion with gold tassels at the corners. The burnished gold is set with tiny purple amethysts and
turquoise stones, and a ring of small gold rosettes runs around the band. A soft purple silk veil is
draped half over one side of the cushion, as if something is hidden underneath.
A single beam of warm golden light falls from above onto the crown; golden dust motes and soft sparkles
float in the beam. The cushion rests in soft, warm darkness that glows deep purple and amber above,
scattered with tiny stars. Faint tall stone columns fade into shadow at the far left and right edges.
WONDER AND MYSTERY: whose crown is this, and what secret is hidden here?

back.objective: **Being brave** even when you feel scared
back.say:
[Hold the card up high] **Look at this crown! Who wears a crown?**
**It belongs to Queen Esther. Esther had a secret… and one day she had to be very, very brave.**
[Fists on hips, chin up] **Let's find out!**

ask.text: What do you see on the crown?
What do you think her secret is?

back.transition: Who is this queen with a secret?

pshat.text: Purim tells how Queen Esther and her cousin Mordechai saved the Jewish people of the Persian Empire. The king put the royal crown on Esther's head and made her queen (2:17), but she did not tell anyone she was Jewish, because Mordechai told her not to (2:10). When the Jewish people needed her, she used her courage. We keep Purim on the 14th of Adar (15th in Jerusalem) (9:20-22).

sages.text: Our Sages teach that Esther's name is hinted at in the Torah's words 'I will surely hide (הַסְתֵּר אַסְתִּיר) My face.' Hashem's name never appears in the whole Megillah, yet Hashem was there, hidden, the whole time. Hidden courage, hidden help: that is the theme of this week.

adapt.see: Bring a real (toy) crown and a scarf; hide the crown under the scarf and reveal it.
adapt.do: Children who don't want to stand can do the brave gesture sitting: fists on hips, chin up.
adapt.join: Everyone can point to the crown, or nod when you ask 'Who wears a crown?'

guide.extend: Secret box: put a small Purim object in a closed box; children ask questions to guess what's hidden.
guide.tip: Teach this week's courage gesture now (fists on hips, chin up) and use it every day, every time someone is brave.

cards.image_prompt:
Esther, chest-up portrait, face centered, hands clasped gently near her heart, a quiet brave smile that
hides a secret. Behind her a tall palace doorway with a rich blue curtain draped to one side and a
glowing amber palace hall beyond. Warm golden light from the right lights her face.
Warm, regal, kind: a queen with a secret that children instantly root for.

back.objective: Brave can mean scared, and doing it anyway
back.say:
[Point to Esther's face] **This is Queen Esther. Sometimes Esther felt a little scared…**
[Shaky hands] **…but she was brave anyway!** [Strong arms!]
**Being brave means doing the right thing, even when you feel scared.**

ask.text: How does Esther's face look?
Show me your brave face!

back.transition: Esther had a cousin who helped her…

pshat.text: Esther (her Hebrew name was Hadassah) had no father or mother. Her cousin Mordechai raised her as his own daughter (2:7). When she became queen she kept her people a secret, as Mordechai told her (2:10). Later she risked her life to save them (4:16).

hard_questions.q: Where were Esther's mommy and daddy?
hard_questions.answer: They weren't alive anymore, so her cousin Mordechai took care of her, like a dad.

adapt.see: Hold up two drawn faces, 'a little scared' and 'brave', and point to each as you say it.
adapt.do: Shaky hands and strong arms can be done sitting; children who don't want to move can nod.
adapt.join: Children can point to Esther, or show a brave face with no words.

guide.extend: Brave chart: each time a child does something brave this week, add a sticker to a paper crown.
guide.tip: Say אַמִּיצָה for Esther and אַמִּיץ for a boy; let children pick the word that fits them.

cards.image_prompt:
Mordechai, chest-up portrait, face centered, hands clasped calmly in front of him, a warm, gentle,
grandfatherly smile and crinkled kind eyes. He stands at the king's gate of ancient Persian Shushan:
behind him a tall straight-sided gateway with a flat stone lintel, flanked by thick mud-brick walls
with flat roofs. Along the wall runs a frieze of glazed bricks in turquoise and royal blue, with a
striding golden lion and a row of white-and-gold rosettes. A slender stone column topped with a
twin-bull capital stands at one side. Through the gateway, date palms and flat-roofed sandstone houses.
Bright blue sky above the flat-topped walls, warm afternoon light on his face. No domes, no pointed or
rounded arches anywhere: every opening is rectangular with a flat lintel.
Wise, trustworthy, solid: like a favorite grandfather who always knows the right thing to do.

back.objective: Mordechai cared for Esther and helped her be brave
back.say:
[Point to Mordechai] **This is Mordechai, Esther's cousin. He took care of Esther, like a dad.** [Hug yourself]
**Later he told her: "Who knows? Maybe you became queen for just this time!"** [Tap your head: think!]

ask.text: Who gives you good advice?
Show me a thinking face!

back.transition: Mordechai always stood up for what was right…

guide_ref.note: for such a time as this

pshat.text: Mordechai was a Jew in Shushan who raised his orphaned cousin Esther as his daughter (2:7). When the Jewish people were in danger, he sent Esther a message: "Who knows, perhaps you became queen for just such a time as this" (4:14), meaning maybe this is the reason you are in the palace.

adapt.see: Show the card next to Esther's card: point to each and say 'cousins'.
adapt.do: Children can hug a stuffed animal instead of themselves.
adapt.join: Children can point to someone in the room who helps them.

guide.extend: Good-advice circle: children tell a friend one helpful idea ('If you're sad, you can…').
guide.tip: Say 'for just this time!' slowly. Ask: what could YOU be just right for?

cards.image_prompt:
In the palace hall, King Achashverosh gently places a golden crown on Esther's head as she sits on a
cushioned bench, hands clasped in her lap, eyes wide: happy and a little nervous. Courtiers watch from
both sides, smiling. Warm light streams through tall windows; rich hangings, glowing oil lamps, and a
high ceiling fading into warm amber haze.
A fairy-tale moment with a secret underneath!

back.objective: Esther becomes queen and keeps a secret
back.say:
**The king chose Esther to be the new queen!** [Put on a pretend crown]
**But Esther had a secret: she was Jewish.** [Finger on lips: shhh!]
**Mordechai said, "Don't tell anyone yet."**
**So Esther kept her secret… shhh!**

ask.text: What was Esther's secret?
Show me how to keep a secret!

hebrew.gesture: both hands make a crown on your head

back.transition: Shhh… can you keep a secret?

pshat.text: The king loved Esther, set the royal crown on her head and made her queen (2:17). Esther did not tell anyone her people, because Mordechai had told her not to (2:10). On the card we say only that the king chose her (sensitivity reframe): Vashti and how the queen was chosen are left out.

hard_questions.q: Why did Esther have to keep a secret?
hard_questions.answer: Mordechai asked her to wait. Sometimes a grown-up we trust says 'not yet', and later it's time to share.
hard_questions.redirect: Who can you tell your big feelings to?

adapt.see: Show a paper crown and put it on a doll or puppet 'Esther'.
adapt.do: Children can mime the crown with one hand, or simply nod.
adapt.join: Everyone joins the 'shhh' with a finger on lips; no words needed.

guide.extend: Whisper game: pass a quiet 'Purim!' around the circle without anyone else hearing.
guide.tip: Make the 'shhh' dramatic and soft; children love a secret. Keep it light: Esther is happy, not afraid, here.

cards.image_prompt:
Outside the king's gate in Shushan: a wide stone gateway with tall columns topped with twin-bull capitals
and a turquoise glazed-brick band of gold rosettes. A row of courtiers kneel and bow low toward Haman,
foreheads to the ground. Mordechai is the ONLY one standing: tall and calm, chin up, hands at his sides,
gently shaking his head no. Haman stands by the gate with his arms crossed tight, nose in the air, cheeks
puffed, a big sulky pout, proud and grumpy like a kid who didn't get his way. Warm afternoon sun, deep
blue sky above the flat-topped gate.
QUIET COURAGE next to GRUMPY PRIDE!

back.say:
**Everyone had to bow down to Haman.** [Everyone bow!]
**But Mordechai said, "I am a Jew. I will not bow."** [Stand up tall!]
**Haman was SO proud, and SO angry!** [Cross arms, grumpy face]
**He made a very bad plan against the Jewish people.**

ask.text: What did Mordechai say?
Show me how Mordechai stood!

hebrew.gesture: stand up straight, hands at sides

back.transition: Uh-oh… the Jewish people need help!

pshat.text: The king ordered everyone at the palace gate to bow to Haman, his top official, but Mordechai would not bow (3:2). He told the courtiers that he was a Jew (3:4). When Haman saw it, he was "filled with rage" (חֵמָה) (3:5): his hurt pride turned into anger. Not satisfied with Mordechai alone, he made a plan against all the Jews in the kingdom (3:6). On the card: "a very bad plan."

sages.text: Our Sages teach that Haman made himself like an idol, a little god for people to bow to, so Mordechai would bow only to Hashem.

hard_questions.q: Did Haman hurt the Jewish people?
hard_questions.answer: No. Haman had a bad plan, but Esther and Mordechai were brave, and the Jewish people were safe.
hard_questions.redirect: Who was brave in our story?

adapt.see: Have one child stand while the others bow, so everyone sees the difference.
adapt.do: Children who can't bow can nod their head down; standing children can just sit up tall.
adapt.join: Everyone can do the grumpy Haman face and crossed arms without speaking.

guide.extend: Feelings talk: 'Haman felt proud and angry. What can we do when we feel angry?' (take a breath, tell a grown-up).
guide.tip: Name Haman's feelings gently (proud, angry) and move on fast; he's grumpy and silly, never scary.

cards.image_prompt:
The king's throne hall in Shushan: tall slender columns with twin-bull capitals, a flat cedar-beam
ceiling glowing with warm light, turquoise and gold glazed-brick rosettes along the walls, purple
hangings. King Achashverosh sits on a tall golden throne, leaning forward with a big surprised, warm
smile, holding out a long golden scepter toward Esther. Esther, in royal purple robes, has just stepped
into the hall: one hand pressed to her heart, the other reaching out to touch the tip of the scepter,
her face brave and relieved. Two courtiers at the side peek out in surprise.
RELIEF AND COURAGE: she was scared, and she did it anyway!

back.objective: Esther was scared, and brave anyway
back.say:
**The grown-ups didn't eat for three days, for Esther.**
**Then she went to the king without being called. Scary!** [Shaky hands…]
**The king held out his golden stick. Phew! The Jewish people were safe!** [Cheer!]

ask.text: How did Esther feel before she went in?
What helped Esther be brave?

back.transition: Hooray! That's why we celebrate Purim!

pshat.text: Anyone who came to the king without being called could be put to death, unless the king held out his golden scepter (4:11). Esther asked all the Jews of Shushan to fast for her for three days, then went in: "and if I perish, I perish" (4:16). The king held out the scepter and she touched its tip (5:1-2). At her feast she asked for her people's lives and named Haman (7:3-6). A king's decree could not be undone (8:8), so a new one let the Jews stand up for themselves (8:11). The day turned around (9:1), and the Jews had light and joy (8:16).

hard_questions.answer: Haman's bad plan didn't work, and he wasn't able to hurt anyone anymore.
hard_questions.redirect: What do you think the Jewish people did to celebrate?

hard_questions.q: Couldn't the king just cancel the bad plan?
hard_questions.answer: In that kingdom, a king's rule could never be erased. So the king made a new rule: the Jewish people could stand up and protect themselves, and they were safe.
hard_questions.redirect: How do we stand up tall and brave?

hard_questions.q: Do I have to stop eating like Esther?
hard_questions.answer: No. Only grown-ups fast, on the day before Purim. Children eat and help in other ways.
hard_questions.redirect: How can YOU help someone this Purim?

adapt.see: Use a real stick or wand as the golden scepter; children touch its tip.
adapt.do: Shaky hands and reaching can be done sitting; a child can hold the 'scepter' for the class.
adapt.join: Everyone joins the cheer, or claps, or shows the brave gesture.

guide.extend: Act it out: one child is the king with the scepter, another walks in bravely; everyone else cheers.
guide.tip: Fasting is for grown-ups only; say so if children ask. 'Scepter' is a new word: 'a king's golden stick'.

cards.image_prompt:
A bright, cozy shul hall decorated for Purim: purple, blue and gold paper streamers and warm pendant
lights hang from the ceiling. A friendly man in a knit kippah with olive skin and a short dark beard
stands at a wooden reading table, reading from ONE parchment scroll that is rolled up on itself with no
wooden handles; the written side faces him, so we see only the plain back of the parchment.
Around him families listen: an Ethiopian Jewish mother with her son in a kippah, an Ashkenazi grandfather
with a white beard and kippah, a Mizrahi girl dressed as a queen. In front, children sit on the floor
shaking colorful groggers high in the air and laughing; boys wear kippot, girls wear dresses; one girl
covers her ears and giggles.
NOISY, HAPPY, TOGETHER!

back.objective: We listen to the Megillah and drown out Haman
back.say:
**On Purim we listen to the Megillah, the story of Esther.** [Hands behind ears]
**When we hear "Haman," we make noise so nobody can hear his name!** [Say "Haman": everyone shakes]
**When I say "Esther"… FREEZE!** [Repeat 3×]

ask.text: What do we do when we hear 'Haman'?
Show me your quietest freeze!

back.transition: What else do we do on Purim?

pshat.text: Mordechai wrote down the story and told the Jews to remember these days every year (9:20-22). We hear the whole Megillah read from a scroll at night and again in the day. A Megillah is one scroll rolled on itself, not on two wooden rollers like a Torah.

sages.text: Making noise at Haman's name is an old custom, so that his name is 'blotted out' and can't be heard; the Rema writes that children do it.

adapt.see: Show a real megillah or a rolled paper scroll; point out it has one roller, not two.
adapt.do: Sound-sensitive children can clap softly or stamp, or cover their ears; that's fine.
adapt.join: Everyone joins the FREEZE; no words needed.

guide.extend: Make groggers: dried beans in a sealed cup or bottle, decorated with stickers.
guide.tip: The FREEZE on 'Esther' gives the noise a clear stop. Practice the stop before you start the noise.

cards.image_prompt:
A sunny front porch of a modern home on Purim. An Ethiopian Jewish boy in a kippah and a lion costume and
his Ashkenazi friend, a girl in a ladybug costume, hold out a basket together to a smiling Sephardi
grandmother who is opening her front door. The basket is wrapped in clear cellophane with a big purple
ribbon and holds hamantaschen, a red apple, a small juice bottle and wrapped candies. The boy's mother,
in a knee-length skirt, waves from the garden path carrying two more baskets. Potted flowers by the door,
blue sky above the roof.
THE JOY OF GIVING!

back.objective: We send Purim food gifts to friends
back.say:
**On Purim we send mishloach manot: food gifts for a friend.** [Hold out a pretend basket]
**Two kinds of food, like a hamantasch and an apple!** [Show two fingers]
**Knock, knock! "Happy Purim!"** [Knock in the air]

ask.text: Who would you send a Purim basket to?
Which two foods would you put inside?

hebrew.gesture: hold out a pretend basket with two hands

pshat.text: Mordechai told the Jews to keep Purim with "sending portions to one another" (מִשְׁלוֹחַ מָנוֹת) (9:22). The happiness of being safe is shared with friends.

sages.text: Our Sages teach that mishloach manot is at least two kinds of ready-to-eat food, sent to at least one person.

adapt.see: Bring a real basket and two foods; count 'one, two!' as you put them in.
adapt.do: Children pass the basket around the circle and say 'Happy Purim!' or just smile.
adapt.join: Everyone can show two fingers for 'two kinds of food'.

guide.extend: Class mishloach manot: each child decorates a paper bag; the class fills them for the school staff.
guide.tip: Check allergies before any real food. Paper or play food works just as well.

cards.image_prompt:
A festive Purim meal at a long family table in a warm dining room, with streamers and balloons above and
warm lamp light. A diverse family in Purim costumes: a Mizrahi dad in a kippah dressed as a king carries
a big platter of food, an Ashkenazi grandmother laughs, an Ethiopian Jewish aunt passes a bowl of grapes,
and children in costumes (a boy in a kippah dressed as a firefighter, a girl dressed as a butterfly) raise
cups of juice. On the table: a braided bread, a plate of hamantaschen, salads and fruit.
In front, a little girl drops a coin into a small plain wooden tzedakah box while her brother in a kippah
holds out another coin, waiting his turn.
GIVING AND CELEBRATING TOGETHER!

back.objective: We help people in need and share a Purim meal
back.say:
**On Purim we give gifts to people who need help, so everyone can be happy.** [Drop a coin in a pretend box]
**Then we eat a big Purim meal with our family!** [Rub your tummy: yum!]
**Giving and celebrating together: that's Purim!**

ask.text: How can we help someone who needs it?
Show me your happiest Purim dance!

hebrew.note: gifts to people in need: מַתָּנוֹת לָאֶבְיוֹנִים

pshat.text: Mordechai told the Jews to keep Purim as "days of feasting and joy" and with "gifts to the poor" (מַתָּנוֹת לָאֶבְיוֹנִים) (9:22). The month had turned from sadness to joy (9:22), and on Purim everyone, rich or poor, should be able to celebrate.

sages.text: Our Sages teach that we give gifts to at least two people in need on Purim day, and that it is better to give more to the poor than to spend more on the meal or on mishloach manot.

hard_questions.answer: Sometimes people don't have enough money for food or things they need. On Purim we make sure they can be happy too.
hard_questions.redirect: What could we give to help?

adapt.see: Bring a real tzedakah box; let each child drop in a play coin.
adapt.do: Children can pass the box around, or the teacher holds it while each child taps it.
adapt.join: Everyone can rub their tummy for 'yum' or dance in place.

guide.extend: Class tzedakah: collect coins all week; the children decide together where the money goes.
guide.tip: Talk about 'people who need help', never 'poor kids'; some families in your class may be struggling.

cards.image_prompt:
Six diverse children sit cross-legged in a circle on a round braided rug with rings of red, blue, yellow
and green. A girl with brown curly hair leans forward, mid-sentence, telling her story. A boy in a striped
kippah raises his hand high, eager to share. An Ethiopian boy in a knit kippah rests his chin on his hands,
listening with wide eyes. A girl with a pink headband hugs her knees, smiling shyly. Two more children
listen, one with a hand on a friend's shoulder. Behind them, a lived-in gan: a low bookshelf with picture
books and a teddy bear, children's drawings on the wall, a plant on a sunny windowsill.
Warm, safe, everyone belongs.

back.objective: Children name a time they were brave
back.say:
**Esther felt scared, and she was brave anyway.** [Share one brave moment of your own]
**Now it's your turn. When were YOU brave?** [Pass the card to whoever is sharing]

ask.text: What did your body feel like?
Point to the face that shows how you felt!

guide_ref.note: if a child shares something hard

pshat.text: Esther was afraid (4:11) and went to the king anyway (4:16). This card links her courage to the children's own lives: a doctor visit, a dark room, saying sorry, trying something new.

hard_questions.q: (A child shares something frightening or sad.)
hard_questions.answer: Thank the child, say 'that sounds hard, and you were brave to tell us', and check in privately later. Tell a parent or the school if needed.
hard_questions.redirect: Who helps you when you feel scared?

adapt.see: Hold up the four feeling faces and let children point.
adapt.do: A child can share by drawing instead of talking.
adapt.join: Children can pass the card without speaking; everyone shows the brave gesture for each sharer.

guide.extend: Brave book: each child draws one brave moment; bind the pages into a class book.
guide.tip: Share a small, real brave moment of your own first; it gives children permission to share.

cards.image_prompt:
Esther takes a brave step forward through a long palace corridor: right hand pressed to her heart, left
hand reaching forward, chin lifted, eyes bright and determined, her robe flowing behind her. She walks
from cool shadow into warm golden light pouring from the throne hall ahead. Tall columns at the edges,
a patterned stone floor.
COURAGE: a small person taking a big brave step!

back.objective: Say and show gibor and giborah: hero!
back.say:
**Our power word is GIBOR: a hero!** [Make strong arms]
**Say it with me: gee-BOR!**
**A boy is a gibor. A girl is a giborah.**
**Esther was a giborah: brave even when scared. Who can be a hero? YOU can!** [Point to everyone]

ask.text: Who can be a gibor or a giborah?
Show me your strong arms!

hebrew.note: for a girl: gee-bo-RAH גִּבּוֹרָה · boy גִּבּוֹר

pshat.text: Esther's courage (4:16) and Mordechai's (3:2) make them heroes of the Purim story. The word gibor is not in the Megillah; it is the Hebrew word for a hero or a strong, brave person.

adapt.see: Write גִּבּוֹר and גִּבּוֹרָה big on the board; point to the one each child chooses.
adapt.do: Children who can't raise their arms can make two fists in their lap.
adapt.join: Everyone shows strong arms together; no words needed.

guide.extend: Hero hunt: all week, catch children being brave and call out 'Gibor!' or 'Giborah!'
guide.tip: Stress the end: gee-BOR, gee-bo-RAH. Let each child choose the word that fits them; never correct a child's choice.

cards.image_prompt:
Not generated: the home card uses the Card Designer's own front. (If art is ever wanted: a diverse family
packing mishloach manot baskets together at a kitchen table, a boy in a kippah tying a ribbon.)

back.objective: We learned about **being brave even when scared**

shabbat_question.en: When were you brave this week?

try_at_home.text: Make mishloach manot together: two foods for a neighbor.
Ask your child to show you the brave gesture: fists on hips, chin up!
Retell the Purim story; stamp your feet at 'Haman'.

pshat.text: On Purim we hear the Megillah, send food gifts to friends, give to people in need and share a festive meal (9:22). The family letter (p.17) explains the week's value, courage, and the word gibor.

adapt.see: Send the card home with a photo of the class's groggers or mishloach manot.
adapt.do: Families who can't deliver food can make a card or drawing for a neighbor instead.
adapt.join: A child who doesn't talk much can show the gesture to the family.

guide.extend: Families send back a photo or drawing of their mishloach manot for a class wall.
guide.tip: Send it home before Purim so families can plan mishloach manot together.
